📳 Baspar Exclusive/ When ships sit idle, what happens beneath the water's surface? Why has the prolonged stoppage of ships in the Persian Gulf once again brought the issue of marine coatings to the fore?🔸 Baspar/Iran Polymer The maritime crisis in the Persian Gulf and restricted traffic along the route leading to the Strait of Hormuz is not merely a matter of scheduling, loading, or cargo delivery. For a ship that remains stationary in the water for weeks or months, some of the most significant changes take place where they cannot be seen from the deck: below the water's surface. The hull surface, in constant contact with seawater — under conditions where the ship has been deprived of its normal movement — enters a biological and hydrodynamic process that can, once the ship returns to its route, manifest as reduced speed, increased engine load, higher fuel consumption, and diminished voyage efficiency.✍️ Golrokh Fard Zolfaghari, PhD student in Polymer Engineering 🔸 A field example of this situation has also been observed with one of the Hapag-Lloyd ships. After six to eight weeks in water at a temperature of about 30 degrees Celsius, this ship encountered a significant amount of biofouling. Biofouling and barnacles had covered the entire surface of the propeller and most of the ship's vertical surfaces, and about 40 percent of the underwater hull surface was also covered with this growth. The company's CEO stated that the amount of biofouling that had developed was such that the ship was forced to move at a lower speed when passing through the Strait of Hormuz.🔸 According to SAFETY4SEA, increased biofouling can lead to reduced ship speed, higher fuel consumption, increased engine load, and greater emissions of pollutants. Therefore, before the ship returns to operation, an underwater inspection must be carried out with a diver or a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) to determine the extent of biofouling and decide on cleaning or corrective measures.🔸 Antifouling coating is a preventive solution ... 🔸 Read the full text here: https://zaya.io/s4oo5◀️ The longest-running specialized news outlet for polymer science and industries and coatings www.iranpolymer.com🆔 Follow us on "WhatsApp":https://chat.whatsapp.com/Cn2vFzFBdv37wTZNPI1Ham?s=cl&p=a&mlu=4&ilr=0🆔 Follow us on Instagram:https://www.instagram.com/basparmag/

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

The play "Cyrus" is not a return to the past for me; it is looking at today through the mirror of history. In writing this play, rather than seeking to construct a mythical figure of Cyrus, I have thought about a human being who, amid power, violence, and fear, faces a difficult choice: the sword or the word. History, for me, is not a mass of names and conquests; it is the memory of the people who lived in it; people who were afraid, who loved, who betrayed, who stood firm, and who made choices at fateful moments. "Cyrus" is an attempt to hear the silenced voices of these very people; to see the human beings who have sometimes been forgotten behind the great names of history. As a director, too, I have not wanted to reconstruct history; I have wanted to summon it into the present; so that perhaps we may realize that the distance between that era and our era is not as far as we think. "Cyrus" is not the narrative of a conqueror; it is the search for a human being who wants to take power beyond the mere meaning of domination. Perhaps that is why, for me, "Cyrus" is more about the possibility of remaining human in the midst of power than about the past.#نادر_برهانی_مرند@moaser_theater
